practiceSet.title: U1.LT2 Practice: Living vs. Non-living
practiceSet.description: Practice the six characteristics of life from class, sorting biotic and abiotic factors, and explaining why some nonliving things can seem alive.

activity.title: U1.LT2 Relearning: Living vs. Non-living
activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can compare and contrast the properties of living organisms (biotic) with non-living (abiotic) entities, providing specific examples for each of the characteristics of life.

**Think of a club with six membership rules.** To join the "Living Club," you must follow all six rules. A snowball rolling downhill seems to follow one rule (it gets bigger), and a phone seems to follow one (it runs on energy from its battery), but neither follows all six, so neither gets in. Neither one even follows the Cells rule: a snowball and a phone have no cells at all.

**The six characteristics of life:**
- **Cells:** made of one or more cells, the basic unit of life. Some organisms are single-celled (a paramecium); others are multicellular (a sunflower, you).
- **Use Energy:** takes in fuel to carry out life activities. Animals eat food (a chickadee eats seeds); plants capture sunlight to make their own food.
- **Reproduction:** makes new organisms of its own kind (a robin lays eggs that hatch into chicks, a potato sprouts new plants from its eyes).
- **Respond to Environment:** reacts to changes around it (a cat's pupils shrink in bright light, a mimosa plant folds its leaves when touched). It happens in **one organism**, during its lifetime (in seconds or over a whole season).
- **Adaptation:** a **population** develops helpful traits over **many generations** (a duck's webbed feet, a porcupine's sharp quills). It happens slowly.
- **Growth and Development:** gets bigger (growth) and changes as it matures (development), like a fuzzy chick growing into a hen.

**Biotic vs. abiotic:** **Biotic** factors are the living parts of an environment (chipmunks, wildflowers, bacteria). **Abiotic** factors are the nonliving parts (air, ice, humidity, clay). Abiotic factors affect biotic ones: a hard frost kills the tomato plants in a garden.

**Living vs. nonliving:** a nonliving thing can seem to show some characteristics (a snowball gets bigger, a phone uses energy), but only a living thing shows **all six**. The quickest way to rule something out is cells: no cells means not alive. But cells alone are not enough; a living thing must show the other five characteristics, too.

**Worked example 1:** Is a freshwater mussel from the Chippewa River living? It looks like a rock and hardly moves. Step 1: Cells? Yes, a mussel is an animal made of cells. Step 2: Use Energy? It filters tiny bits of food out of the water. Step 3: Reproduction? It releases tiny young that grow into new mussels. Step 4: Growth and Development? A tiny young mussel grows into an adult with a bigger, thicker shell. Step 5: Respond to Environment? It clamps its shell shut when the water gets muddy. Step 6: Adaptation? Over many generations, mussels developed hard shells that protect them from many predators. **Answer:** a mussel shows all six, so it is living (biotic), even though it looks like a rock and hardly moves.

**Worked example 2:** Respond or adapt? (a) A painted turtle climbs onto a log to warm up in the sun on a cool morning. One turtle, in minutes, so it is **Respond to Environment**. (b) Over many generations, snowshoe hares developed big, furry feet that keep them from sinking into deep snow. A population, over generations, so it is **Adaptation**. The clues are the time and whether it is one organism or a population.

**Worked example 3:** A sand dune on the Lake Michigan shore gets bigger and creeps across the beach. Is it alive? Step 1: Cells? No, it is a pile of sand grains. Step 2: Does it use energy, reproduce, or respond? No; the wind piles up the sand and pushes it along. Step 3: It seems to show one life-like trait (getting bigger), and moving is not one of the six characteristics. **Answer:** nonliving (abiotic).

**Watch out for:** calling something alive just because it moves or grows (rivers, snowballs, wind-up toys); thinking anything made of cells must be alive (a fallen log or a wooden table is made of cells from a tree, but those cells are dead, so it no longer uses energy, grows, or responds); thinking all living things must move or breathe air (pine trees don't walk around, and some bacteria live without oxygen); mixing up Respond to Environment (one organism, within its lifetime) and Adaptation (a population, over many generations); thinking one animal can develop an adaptation by trying hard; forgetting that a single cell, like a paramecium, is fully alive; and forgetting that things organisms need, like air and water, are still abiotic.
prompts: List the six characteristics of life. For each one, give a specific example from an organism that lives in Wisconsin.
Explain why a river is not alive even though it moves and gets bigger after a storm. Name the characteristics it seems to show and the ones it is missing.
Explain the difference between Respond to Environment and Adaptation. Give one example of each.
Name three biotic factors and three abiotic factors in a Wisconsin lake. Then describe one way an abiotic factor affects a biotic factor.
